ENG-P1.title: Original Passage
ENG-P1.content: At a coastal high school, students built a simple rain gauge network using identical containers placed in open locations. Each group measured rainfall at the same time every day. After one month, the class compared the results and found that gauges near tall buildings consistently collected less water. They concluded that placement can affect measurements and decided to relocate those gauges before the next observation period.

ENG-P2.title: Original Passage
ENG-P2.content: A barangay library introduced a tool-lending corner where residents could borrow basic repair equipment. The program did not replace professional services; instead, it helped households complete small tasks such as tightening loose hinges or assembling shelves. Borrowers attended a short safety orientation, and damaged tools were inspected before being returned to circulation.

ENG-P3.title: Original Passage
ENG-P3.content: Many people assume that a brighter screen is always easier to read. In a dim room, however, excessive brightness can create glare and eye discomfort. Readability depends not only on brightness but also on contrast, text size, viewing distance, and surrounding light. A comfortable setting is therefore one that matches the environment rather than simply maximizing brightness.

ENG-P4.title: Original Passage
ENG-P4.content: A student research team tested two methods of drying fruit slices. Method A used direct sunlight, while Method B used a ventilated solar dryer with a transparent cover. The covered dryer reached a higher temperature and protected the fruit from dust, but it required careful airflow control to prevent moisture from becoming trapped. The team concluded that design details, not heat alone, determine drying performance.

W2-ENG-P1.title: Cooling a Classroom
W2-ENG-P1.content:
A school tested three low-cost ways to reduce afternoon heat in a west-facing classroom. Curtains lowered glare but trapped warm air when the windows were closed. A reflective film reduced solar heating but also made the room slightly darker. Exterior shade cloth produced the largest temperature reduction while allowing windows to remain open.

The team concluded that no single feature should be judged in isolation. Thermal comfort depends on heat gain, ventilation, lighting, and how the room is actually used.

W2-ENG-P2.title: Shared Bicycle Repair Station
W2-ENG-P2.content:
A university installed a small bicycle repair station near the main gate. The station included a pump and basic tools attached by cables. During the first month, users frequently returned the tools to the wrong positions, so maintenance staff added labeled outlines and brief instructions.

Tool loss did not increase, but repair time became shorter because users could identify the correct tool more quickly. The change illustrates how clear visual organization can improve a public service without adding expensive equipment.

W2-ENG-P3.title: Citizen Rainfall Reports
W2-ENG-P3.content:
Residents in several upland communities began sending rainfall measurements to a shared online map. At first, containers differed in shape and some observations were taken at irregular times. The map looked detailed, but the values were difficult to compare.

After volunteers distributed identical gauges and set a common observation time, the reports became more useful. The experience showed that large amounts of data do not automatically produce reliable information; consistency in collection is equally important.

W2-ENG-P4.title: Composting Trial
W2-ENG-P4.content:
Two compost piles contained the same mixture of leaves and food scraps. One pile was turned every three days, while the other was left undisturbed. The turned pile heated quickly and decomposed faster, but it also dried out and required additional water.

The students learned that aeration can accelerate decomposition, yet moisture must still be monitored. A treatment that improves one condition may create a new limitation.

W2-ENG-P5.title: Library Noise Zones
W2-ENG-P5.content:
A library divided its study area into silent, quiet-discussion, and collaborative zones. Signs alone were not enough: users often chose the nearest table without noticing the zone. The library then changed furniture layout and floor markings so that each area looked and felt different.

Complaints decreased after the redesign. The result suggests that behavior is influenced not only by written rules but also by how a space communicates its intended use.

W3-VRPASS-001.title: Short Reasoning Passage 1
W3-VRPASS-001.content: A barangay installed rain barrels at three buildings. Water use for cleaning fell, but the barrels overflowed during intense storms. The project team added first-flush diverters and larger overflow pipes before expanding the program.
W3-VRPASS-001.source_note: Original TutoDemy stimulus; not copied or traced from a protected source.

W3-VRPASS-002.title: Short Reasoning Passage 2
W3-VRPASS-002.content: A laboratory repeated a measurement with two instruments. Both were precise, but one consistently read 0.4 units high. Calibration corrected the offset.
W3-VRPASS-002.source_note: Original TutoDemy stimulus; not copied or traced from a protected source.

W3-VRPASS-003.title: Short Reasoning Passage 3
W3-VRPASS-003.content: A library survey found that users wanted longer hours, but attendance data showed very low use during the final hour on most days. The staff decided to test extended hours only during examination weeks.
W3-VRPASS-003.source_note: Original TutoDemy stimulus; not copied or traced from a protected source.

W3-VRPASS-004.title: Short Reasoning Passage 4
W3-VRPASS-004.content: A coastal village restored mangroves and also moved critical equipment to higher ground. After a storm, damage was lower than in previous years, but the report did not claim either measure alone caused the improvement.
W3-VRPASS-004.source_note: Original TutoDemy stimulus; not copied or traced from a protected source.

W3-VRPASS-005.title: Short Reasoning Passage 5
W3-VRPASS-005.content: A school tested two schedules for laboratory classes. The shorter schedule reduced idle time but left too little time for cleanup. The revised schedule kept the efficient setup sequence and restored a dedicated cleanup period.
W3-VRPASS-005.source_note: Original TutoDemy stimulus; not copied or traced from a protected source.

W3-VRPASS-006.title: Short Reasoning Passage 6
W3-VRPASS-006.content: A researcher mapped urban temperatures using sensors placed at different heights. The results varied widely until all sensors were mounted at a common height and shielded from direct sunlight.
W3-VRPASS-006.source_note: Original TutoDemy stimulus; not copied or traced from a protected source.

W3-VRPASS-007.title: Short Reasoning Passage 7
W3-VRPASS-007.content: A community garden used compost from several sources. Plant growth varied, so the team measured nutrient content and adjusted application rates rather than assuming all compost was equivalent.
W3-VRPASS-007.source_note: Original TutoDemy stimulus; not copied or traced from a protected source.

W3-VRPASS-008.title: Short Reasoning Passage 8
W3-VRPASS-008.content: A student argues that a battery is better because it powered one device longer. The teacher asks whether both devices had the same power demand.
W3-VRPASS-008.source_note: Original TutoDemy stimulus; not copied or traced from a protected source.

W3-ENG-P1.title: Low-Cost Air Monitoring
W3-ENG-P1.content:
Students placed low-cost air-quality sensors near a road, a garden, and an indoor corridor. At first, the roadside sensor appeared to record the highest particle level at all hours. The team later discovered that it was mounted close to an exhaust vent from a small generator.

After relocating the sensor and repeating the measurements, roadside values were still elevated during rush hour but no longer remained high throughout the day. The experience showed that a plausible result can still be distorted by poor sensor placement.

W3-ENG-P2.title: Community Seed Bank
W3-ENG-P2.content:
A farming cooperative created a seed bank to preserve locally adapted crop varieties. Members contributed seeds after each harvest, but early records listed only crop names. When some packets failed to germinate, the cooperative began recording collection date, source farm, moisture condition, and germination-test results.

The additional information allowed members to identify old or poorly stored seed before distribution. The project became more useful not because it stored more packets, but because its records made the collection interpretable.

W3-ENG-P3.title: Reflective Roof Trial
W3-ENG-P3.content:
Two similar classrooms received different roof treatments. One roof was coated with a reflective material, while the other remained unchanged. During clear afternoons, the treated room was cooler, but the difference was smaller on cloudy days.

The investigators concluded that the coating reduced solar heat gain, yet its benefit depended on weather conditions. They recommended monitoring over a full season before estimating annual energy savings.

W3-ENG-P4.title: Repairable Electronics
W3-ENG-P4.content:
A student group compared two portable lamps. Lamp A was cheaper and lighter, but its battery was glued inside the case. Lamp B used screws and a replaceable battery, although it cost more initially.

The group argued that purchase price alone does not determine value. Products that can be repaired may last longer and create less waste, but the benefit depends on the availability and price of replacement parts.

W3-ENG-P5.title: Wetland Walkway
W3-ENG-P5.content:
A nature reserve planned a raised walkway through a wetland. The shortest route crossed an area used by nesting birds, while a longer route followed previously disturbed ground. Engineers also considered seasonal flooding and maintenance access.

The final design was not the shortest path. It was selected because it reduced ecological disturbance and remained accessible for inspection. The decision illustrates that design optimization often involves several objectives rather than one.

W4-VRPASS-001.title: Wave 4 Reasoning Passage 1
W4-VRPASS-001.content: A municipality installed water-level sensors in several drainage canals. Early alerts improved response time, but false alarms occurred when floating debris covered the sensors. The maintenance plan was revised to include protective screens and scheduled cleaning.
W4-VRPASS-001.source_note: Original TutoDemy stimulus; not copied or traced from a protected source.

W4-VRPASS-002.title: Wave 4 Reasoning Passage 2
W4-VRPASS-002.content: A laboratory measured the same standard solution with two pipettes. One produced tightly grouped values that were consistently low. Recalibration corrected the offset.
W4-VRPASS-002.source_note: Original TutoDemy stimulus; not copied or traced from a protected source.

W4-VRPASS-003.title: Wave 4 Reasoning Passage 3
W4-VRPASS-003.content: A library considered opening two hours later every day. Attendance records showed strong late demand only during examination periods, so the library tested extended hours during those weeks first.
W4-VRPASS-003.source_note: Original TutoDemy stimulus; not copied or traced from a protected source.

W4-VRPASS-004.title: Wave 4 Reasoning Passage 4
W4-VRPASS-004.content: A coastal town built a seawall and restored dunes. After a storm, damage was lower, but investigators also noted that the storm followed a different path than previous storms.
W4-VRPASS-004.source_note: Original TutoDemy stimulus; not copied or traced from a protected source.

W4-VRPASS-005.title: Wave 4 Reasoning Passage 5
W4-VRPASS-005.content: A school shortened a laboratory activity to reduce waiting time. Students completed the procedure faster, but cleanup errors increased. The revised plan kept the efficient setup while restoring a separate cleanup checklist.
W4-VRPASS-005.source_note: Original TutoDemy stimulus; not copied or traced from a protected source.

W4-VRPASS-006.title: Wave 4 Reasoning Passage 6
W4-VRPASS-006.content: Researchers compared temperature readings from sensors mounted on walls, roofs, and shaded posts. They standardized height and shielding before interpreting location differences.
W4-VRPASS-006.source_note: Original TutoDemy stimulus; not copied or traced from a protected source.

W4-VRPASS-007.title: Wave 4 Reasoning Passage 7
W4-VRPASS-007.content: A cooperative tested compost from several suppliers. Plant growth varied, so the team measured nitrogen content and moisture before comparing application rates.
W4-VRPASS-007.source_note: Original TutoDemy stimulus; not copied or traced from a protected source.

W4-VRPASS-008.title: Wave 4 Reasoning Passage 8
W4-VRPASS-008.content: A student says one battery brand is better because it lasted longer in a flashlight. The teacher asks whether both flashlights used the same bulb and brightness setting.
W4-VRPASS-008.source_note: Original TutoDemy stimulus; not copied or traced from a protected source.

W4-VRPASS-009.title: Wave 4 Reasoning Passage 9
W4-VRPASS-009.content: Flood reports cluster near a low-lying district with narrow drains. Engineers review both elevation and drain capacity before choosing a solution.

W4-ENG-P1.title: River Temperature Sensors
W4-ENG-P1.content:
A student team placed temperature sensors at three points along a small river. The downstream sensor showed unusually high midday readings. At first, the team suspected warm discharge from nearby buildings.

A site visit revealed that the downstream sensor was in shallow water exposed to direct sunlight, while the other sensors were shaded. After the sensors were installed at similar depths and with comparable shielding, the downstream site remained slightly warmer but the extreme difference disappeared. The investigation showed that environmental measurements must distinguish site effects from instrument placement effects.

W4-ENG-P2.title: Tool-Lending Library
W4-ENG-P2.content:
A community opened a tool-lending library so residents could borrow equipment used only occasionally. Early membership grew quickly, but several tools were returned damaged because borrowers lacked experience.

The organizers responded by adding short safety orientations, illustrated instructions, and maintenance checks. Borrowing slowed slightly, yet the tools lasted longer and injury reports declined. The program's success therefore depended not only on access, but also on guidance and upkeep.

W4-ENG-P3.title: Cool Pavement Trial
W4-ENG-P3.content:
Two parking areas of similar size were resurfaced with different materials. One used a light-colored coating, while the other retained dark asphalt. During sunny afternoons, the coated surface was cooler, but nighttime temperatures became similar.

The investigators concluded that the coating reduced daytime solar heating. They did not claim it lowered temperature at all hours, and they recommended studying glare, durability, and maintenance before wider installation.

W4-ENG-P4.title: Reusable Packaging
W4-ENG-P4.content:
A food cooperative compared disposable containers with reusable ones. Reusable containers required more material and washing, but they could be used many times. Disposable containers required little washing but generated more solid waste.

The cooperative concluded that reuse is not automatically better under every condition. The result depends on how many times a container is actually reused, how it is washed, and how far it is transported.

W4-ENG-P5.title: Hillside Footpath
W4-ENG-P5.content:
A park planned a footpath across a steep hillside. The shortest route climbed directly upward, but it would have required extensive steps and erosion control. A longer route followed the contour and passed through more stable ground.

The final route was longer in distance but gentler in slope. It reduced construction difficulty and runoff risk while remaining accessible to more visitors. The choice illustrates that the shortest route is not always the most practical route.
